messages.content: What is the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics?

Microeconomics and macroeconomics are the two main branches of economics, operating at different levels of aggregation. Microeconomics studies the behaviour of individual economic agents — consumers, households, firms, and markets — and how they make decisions about resource allocation under scarcity. Key questions: how do consumers maximise utility? How do firms maximise profit? How do prices and quantities emerge in markets? How do markets fail? Core tools and concepts: supply and demand analysis, consumer theory (utility functions, budget constraints, indifference curves), producer theory (production functions, cost curves, profit maximisation), market structures (perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition), game theory (strategic interactions between agents), welfare economics (consumer and producer surplus, Pareto efficiency, Pareto improvements), market failures and externalities. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — aggregate phenomena and economy-wide variables. Key questions: what determines the overall level of output (GDP)? What causes unemployment? What determines the price level and inflation? How does monetary policy affect the economy? What causes business cycles (booms and recessions)? Core tools and concepts: national income accounting (GDP = C + I + G + NX), aggregate demand and supply, IS-LM model (goods market + money market equilibrium), AS-AD model, business cycle theory, monetary policy (central bank interest rate setting, money supply), fiscal policy (government spending and taxation), inflation and Phillips curve, economic growth models (Solow, endogenous growth), international economics (balance of payments, exchange rates, trade). The connection: macroeconomic phenomena emerge from aggregated microeconomic behaviour, but micro and macro often use different analytical frameworks.
What is supply and demand and how are equilibrium prices determined?

Supply and demand is the foundational model of how prices and quantities are determined in markets in a decentralised economy. Demand: the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant (ceteris paribus). The demand curve is typically downward sloping — as price rises, quantity demanded falls (the law of demand) due to substitution effects (other goods become relatively cheaper) and income effects (the consumer is effectively poorer). Demand shifters (move the entire curve): income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), consumer preferences, expectations, and number of buyers. Supply: the quantity that producers are willing and able to sell at each price. The supply curve is typically upward sloping — higher prices make production more profitable, incentivising more production. Supply shifters: input costs, technology, number of sellers, government taxes/subsidies, expectations. Market equilibrium: the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — the market clears. At prices above equilibrium: excess supply (surplus) → producers lower prices. At prices below equilibrium: excess demand (shortage) → consumers bid up prices. Market forces push toward equilibrium. Price controls: price ceiling (maximum price below equilibrium — causes persistent shortage; e.g., rent control): QD > QS. Price floor (minimum price above equilibrium — causes persistent surplus; e.g., minimum wage): QS > QD. Elasticity: price elasticity of demand = % change in QD / % change in P. Elastic demand (|Ed| > 1): revenue falls with price increases. Inelastic (|Ed| < 1): revenue rises with price increases. Determinants: availability of substitutes, necessity vs. luxury, proportion of income, time horizon. Cross-price elasticity: positive (substitutes), negative (complements). Income elasticity: positive (normal goods), negative (inferior goods).
What is GDP and how is it measured?

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given time period (typically a year or quarter). 'Final' means goods purchased for ultimate use, not for further processing (to avoid double-counting intermediates). 'Domestic' means within national borders regardless of the nationality of the producer. Three equivalent approaches: (1) Expenditure approach (most common): GDP = C + I + G + NX. C = private consumption (households' spending on goods and services — typically 60-70% of GDP in developed countries); I = gross investment (business spending on capital goods like machinery, buildings, inventory — not financial investment); G = government spending on goods and services (not transfer payments like pensions — these don't represent production); NX = net exports = exports - imports. (2) Income approach: GDP = employee compensation + gross operating surplus (profits) + taxes on production and imports - subsidies. Gross National Income (GNI) = GDP + net income from abroad (different if many foreigners work domestically or citizens work abroad). (3) Production (output) approach: sum of value added at each stage of production — value added = output value - cost of intermediate inputs. This avoids double-counting. Nominal vs. real GDP: nominal GDP uses current prices (affected by both output changes and price changes); real GDP holds prices constant at a base year — measures actual output changes. GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. GDP limitations: excludes non-market activity (unpaid domestic work, volunteer work — Coyle's 'GDP: A Brief but Affectionate History'); doesn't measure distribution of income (high GDP can coexist with high inequality); ignores environmental degradation; misses wellbeing and quality of life. Alternative measures: HDI (Human Development Index — combines income, education, health), GNH (Gross National Happiness — Bhutan).
What are the causes and effects of inflation?

Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level — a fall in the purchasing power of money. It is measured by price indices: CPI (Consumer Price Index — tracks a basket of goods and services typical of household consumption), PCE deflator (Personal Consumption Expenditure — the Federal Reserve's preferred measure), and PPI (Producer Price Index — measures input costs for producers). Causes: (1) Demand-pull inflation: total demand in the economy (aggregate demand) exceeds total supply (aggregate supply). 'Too much money chasing too few goods.' Causes: excessive government spending, loose monetary policy (very low interest rates → more credit → more spending), consumer confidence boom, exports boom. (2) Cost-push inflation: supply-side shocks raise production costs — firms pass cost increases to consumers. Examples: oil price shocks (1973 OPEC embargo, 2022 Russia-Ukraine), supply chain disruptions (COVID-19), wage growth outpacing productivity. (3) Built-in (wage-price spiral): workers expect future inflation and demand higher nominal wages; this increases firms' costs, which are passed on as higher prices, validating workers' expectations — self-fulfilling. (4) Monetary factors: excessive money supply growth (Friedman: 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' — valid for hyperinflation episodes). Effects: (1) Redistribution: debtors benefit (debt value eroded); creditors and savers lose. Fixed-income earners lose real purchasing power. (2) Menu costs: businesses must constantly update prices. (3) Shoe-leather costs: people hold less cash, making more trips to the bank. (4) Uncertainty: reduces investment and long-term planning. (5) Hyperinflation: destroys economic activity (Weimar Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008 — Zimbabwe abandoned its currency). Central bank response: raise interest rates (makes borrowing more expensive → reduces spending → cools inflation). The Taylor Rule provides a framework.
What is monetary policy and how does a central bank control it?

Monetary policy is the set of actions by a central bank (Federal Reserve in the US, Bank of England in UK, ECB in the Eurozone) to control the money supply and interest rates to achieve macroeconomic objectives — typically price stability (inflation target around 2%), full employment, and financial stability. Policy tools: (1) Policy interest rate: the most important tool in modern central banking. The Fed sets the federal funds rate (the rate at which banks lend reserves to each other overnight); Bank of England sets the Bank Rate. By raising the rate: banks raise their own lending rates → mortgages and business loans become more expensive → investment and consumption fall → aggregate demand falls → inflation decreases (at the cost of slower growth). By cutting rates: the opposite — stimulates borrowing and spending. Transmission mechanism: policy rate → market interest rates → asset prices and exchange rates → aggregate demand and output → inflation. (2) Open market operations (OMO): the central bank buys government securities (bonds) from banks (expansionary — injects reserves, lowers the fed funds rate) or sells securities (contractionary). This is the primary mechanism for implementing the target rate. (3) Quantitative easing (QE): when the policy rate hits zero (the zero lower bound — ZLB), the central bank buys longer-term assets (government bonds, mortgage-backed securities) to further lower long-term rates and inject liquidity. Used extensively after the 2008 financial crisis and COVID-19. (4) Reserve requirements: the fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves — rarely used to actively conduct monetary policy in developed countries (reserve requirements dropped to zero in the US in 2020). (5) Forward guidance: communicating future policy intentions to influence expectations and long-term rates (central banks are 'management of expectations').
What is comparative advantage and why does it support free trade?

Comparative advantage is the principle, developed by David Ricardo in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817), that trade is beneficial even when one country is better at producing everything than another country, as long as countries specialise in the goods they produce at relatively lower opportunity cost. Absolute advantage: a country produces more of a good with the same resources. Comparative advantage: a country produces a good at lower opportunity cost (what must be given up to produce it). Classic example: England and Portugal producing cloth and wine. Even if Portugal can produce both more efficiently, England should specialise in cloth if it gives up fewer units of wine per unit of cloth than Portugal does. Portugal specialises in wine. Both trade and both consume more than in autarky. The key insight: trade creates gains from specialisation — the world produces more total output. Opportunity cost determines what to specialise in, not absolute productivity. Ricardo's model: 2 countries, 2 goods, labour as only input. Heckscher-Ohlin model: extends comparative advantage to multiple factors of production — countries export goods that intensively use their abundant factors (capital-abundant countries export capital-intensive goods; labour-abundant countries export labour-intensive goods). Stolper-Samuelson: trade benefits the owners of abundant factors and hurts owners of scarce factors — explaining why globalisation produces winners and losers within countries. Empirical support: free trade agreements are associated with higher GDP, lower consumer prices, greater product variety (Krugman's new trade theory — love of variety, economies of scale). Limitations: factor mobility across sectors is slow; adjustment costs for workers in declining industries are real; trade in imperfect markets (monopolies, externalities) may require intervention; national security and strategic industry arguments.
What is game theory and what is the Nash equilibrium?

Game theory is the mathematical study of strategic decision-making — situations where the outcome for each player depends on the choices of all players. Developed formally by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern (1944), and Nash (1950). A game consists of: players, strategies (the possible choices), and payoffs (the outcomes for each combination of strategies). Nash equilibrium (Nash, 1950): a set of strategies — one for each player — such that no player has an incentive to unilaterally deviate given the strategies of the other players. No player can improve their payoff by changing their strategy alone. Prisoner's Dilemma: two suspects are interrogated separately. If both cooperate (stay silent): each gets 1 year. If both defect (confess): each gets 3 years. If one defects while the other cooperates: defector goes free (0 years), cooperator gets 5 years. Nash equilibrium: both defect (mutual defection dominates — regardless of what the other does, each player prefers to defect). Yet both would be better off if both cooperated (Pareto optimal outcome) — the classic social dilemma. This explains why cooperation is difficult without communication, binding agreements, or repeated interaction. Dominant strategy: a strategy that yields the highest payoff regardless of what others do — if it exists, rational players always play it. Mixed strategy Nash equilibrium: when no pure strategy equilibrium exists (rock-paper-scissors), players randomise. In matching pennies, the NE is to randomise 50/50. Applications: market competition (Cournot and Bertrand oligopoly models), auctions (vickrey auction design), public goods provision, arms races and nuclear deterrence, evolutionary biology (evolutionary stable strategies), negotiation and bargaining (Nash bargaining solution), financial markets (expectations and herding).
What causes economic recessions and how do they end?

An economic recession is a significant decline in economic activity across the economy, typically defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth, lasting more than a few months. The NBER (National Bureau of Economic Research) uses a broader definition in the US: a significant decline in activity spread across the economy, in GDP, income, employment, industrial production, and sales. Causes: (1) Demand shocks: a sudden drop in aggregate demand. Examples: consumer confidence collapses (panicked saving); investment collapses (credit crunch — 2008 financial crisis: banks stopped lending after toxic assets (mortgage-backed securities) collapsed in value); financial crises (bank failures → credit freeze → spending collapses). (2) Supply shocks: a sudden drop in aggregate supply (ability to produce). Examples: oil price shocks (1973, 1979 — dramatically raised production costs); COVID-19 supply chain disruptions and output collapse. (3) Monetary policy errors: excessively tight monetary policy (high interest rates → reduced investment and consumption). The Great Depression (1929-1939): bank failures, money supply contraction (the Federal Reserve failed to prevent it — Friedman and Schwartz's analysis, confirmed by Bernanke), tariff increases (Smoot-Hawley), and debt deflation (Fisher's debt-deflation theory — falling prices increased real debt burden, causing further defaults). How recessions end: (1) Automatic stabilisers: government spending automatically increases during recessions (unemployment benefits, welfare programmes) while taxes automatically fall (lower income → lower tax revenue) — providing a cushion to demand. (2) Monetary stimulus: central banks cut interest rates and/or implement QE to encourage borrowing and spending. (3) Fiscal stimulus: government increases spending or cuts taxes deliberately (Keynesian multiplier). (4) Natural recovery: inventories drawn down; investment picks up; confidence returns; the business cycle turns.
How does monetary policy work — central banks, interest rates, and inflation?

MONETARY POLICY — Central Banks and the Money Supply

THE CENTRAL BANK:
Controls money supply and interest rates to achieve macroeconomic goals.
US: Federal Reserve (Fed). UK: Bank of England. EU: European Central Bank.
Goals (typically): price stability (2% inflation target) + maximum employment.

THE INTEREST RATE (policy rate):
The Fed''s main tool. The Federal Funds Rate: interest banks charge each other overnight.
When Fed raises rate -> all other rates rise (mortgages, car loans, business loans, credit cards).
When Fed cuts rate -> all rates fall.

TRANSMISSION MECHANISM:
Rate UP -> borrowing more expensive:
 Consumers: less mortgage borrowing, less spending, less credit card use.
 Businesses: less investment (projects that were profitable now aren''t at higher rate).
 Effect: less spending -> less demand -> less upward pressure on prices -> inflation falls.
 Also: higher rate -> more attractive to hold US dollars -> dollar appreciates.

Rate DOWN -> borrowing cheaper:
 More consumer spending. More business investment.
 Effect: more demand -> economic stimulus -> helps during recession.

INFLATION:
Too much money chasing too few goods. Prices rise.
Causes: demand-pull (economy overheating), cost-push (oil price shock), monetary (print too much).
Measured by: CPI (Consumer Price Index) — basket of typical consumer goods.
Core CPI: excludes volatile food and energy prices (better underlying trend indicator).

Hyperinflation: extreme case. Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008), Venezuela (2018).
Causes: excessive money printing, loss of confidence in currency.
Fix: drastic austerity, currency reform, external support (IMF).

QUANTITATIVE EASING (QE):
When rate is already 0%, central bank still needs to stimulate.
Fed buys government bonds and mortgage-backed securities.
Effect: increases money supply, drives down long-term rates, pushes investors into riskier assets.
Used extensively: 2008 GFC, 2020 COVID.
Controversy: inflates asset prices (benefits wealthy), potential inflation risk.

QUANTITATIVE TIGHTENING (QT):
Reverse: central bank sells assets, reduces balance sheet, removes money from system.
Used to fight inflation after QE.

MONEY MULTIPLIER:
Banks hold fraction of deposits as reserves, lend rest (fractional reserve banking).
$1000 deposit -> bank lends $900 (10% reserve) -> deposited -> $810 lent -> etc.
Multiplier: 1/reserve_ratio. 10% reserve -> multiplier of 10.
Original $1000 -> creates $10,000 in total money supply.

2008 FINANCIAL CRISIS LESSON:
Excessive risk, leverage, and interconnection. Fed cut rates to 0%.
When banks failed -> credit froze -> recession.
Solution: massive QE, bank bailouts, fiscal stimulus.
Regulation tightened: Dodd-Frank Act, Basel III (higher capital requirements).
How do exchange rates work and what moves them?

EXCHANGE RATES — the price of one currency in terms of another.

HOW IT WORKS:
EUR/USD = 1.08 means 1 euro buys 1.08 US dollars.
To buy euros with dollars: pay 1/1.08 = $0.926 per cent (GBP/USD = "cable").

WHAT MOVES EXCHANGE RATES:
1. INTEREST RATES:
Higher rates attract foreign capital seeking returns.
If US rates rise vs Eurozone: investors sell euros, buy dollars -> dollar appreciates.
Carry trade: borrow low-rate currency, invest in high-rate currency. Risky on reversal.

2. INFLATION:
High inflation erodes purchasing power -> currency depreciates.
Purchasing Power Parity (PPP): exchange rates should equalise prices internationally.
If Big Mac costs $5 in US, £4 in UK: PPP rate = $5/£4 = 1.25. If actual = 1.30: pound overvalued.

3. CURRENT ACCOUNT:
Deficit: imports > exports. Must borrow from abroad or sell assets -> currency weakens.
Surplus: exports > imports. Accumulates foreign assets -> currency strengthens.
US runs persistent current account deficit (world buys more from US... wait, opposite).
US deficit: imports more than exports. Demand for other currencies. But dollar stays strong due to reserve currency status.

4. SPECULATION AND SENTIMENT:
Most FX volume is speculative, not trade. $7.5 trillion daily turnover.
Risk-off: investors flee to safe havens (USD, JPY, CHF) -> these appreciate.
George Soros broke the Bank of England (1992): shorted GBP, forcing UK to exit ERM.

5. GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION:
Central banks can intervene: sell own currency to weaken, buy to strengthen.
China manages CNY: People''s Bank of China intervenes to keep rate in target range.

FIXED vs FLOATING:
Floating: market-determined. USD, EUR, GBP, JPY.
Fixed/pegged: government sets rate. Saudi riyal pegged to USD. Hong Kong Dollar.
Managed float: intervention when rate moves too far. China, India.
Currency union: single currency. Eurozone (can''t adjust exchange rate per country).
Explain unemployment — types, measurement, and policies.

UNEMPLOYMENT — one of the two main macroeconomic concerns (with inflation).

MEASUREMENT:
Unemployment rate: (unemployed / labor force) × 100.
Labor force: employed + unemployed actively seeking work.
NOT counted: retired, students, homemakers, discouraged workers (stopped looking).

US Bureau of Labor Statistics: monthly survey of ~60,000 households.
U-3: "headline" unemployment rate (official). ~3-5% is considered "full employment."
U-6: broader measure includes: part-timers who want full-time, discouraged workers. Often 2× U-3.

TYPES:

FRICTIONAL: temporary between jobs. Normal and healthy.
 Workers leaving jobs to find better ones. New graduates searching.
 Cannot be eliminated (search takes time). ~1-2% of unemployment.

STRUCTURAL: skills mismatch between workers and available jobs.
 Coal miners when coal declines. Factory workers as automation increases.
 Retraining needed. Slow to resolve. Regional: rust belt decline.
 May take years. Not solvable by stimulus alone — need education/retraining policies.

CYCLICAL: due to economic downturns. Too little aggregate demand.
 Demand falls -> firms lay off workers -> workers spend less -> more layoffs.
 Rises in recessions, falls in booms.
 Fix: fiscal stimulus (government spending) or monetary easing (lower interest rates).

SEASONAL: predictable seasonal patterns.
 Lifeguards, farm workers, ski instructors, retail workers.
 BLS adjusts statistics for seasonality.

NATURAL RATE OF UNEMPLOYMENT: frictional + structural. ~4-5% in US.
When unemployment below natural rate: labour market tight, wages rise, inflation risk.
NAIRU: Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment. Below it -> inflation accelerates.

POLICIES:
Reduce cyclical: stimulus spending, lower interest rates, unemployment benefits (maintain spending).
Reduce structural: job retraining, education reform, relocation assistance, apprenticeships.
Reduce frictional: better job matching (LinkedIn effect), employment agencies.
What is globalisation — benefits, costs, and backlash?

GLOBALISATION — increasing integration of world economies, cultures, and societies.

ECONOMIC DIMENSIONS:
Trade: $28 trillion in global goods and services trade (2022). Grew 30× since 1950.
Investment: multinationals operate across borders. $1.3 trillion FDI flows annually.
Finance: capital flows instantly. $7.5 trillion currency traded daily.
Supply chains: iPhone designed in US, components from 43 countries, assembled in China.
Labour: offshoring (outsource to other countries), migration of workers.

BENEFITS:
Ricardo''s comparative advantage: countries specialise in what they do relatively best.
 Total output higher even if one country is absolutely better at everything.
Lower prices: global competition keeps prices down. Consumer surplus.
Developing countries: hundreds of millions lifted from poverty (China: 800M since 1978).
Innovation: technology spread across borders. Scientific collaboration.
Peace: economically integrated countries less likely to go to war (liberal peace theory).

COSTS AND CRITICISMS:
Inequality within developed countries: manufacturing jobs offshored. Workers in Detroit vs shareholders.
Winner-take-all: global tech platforms (Google, Amazon) dominate everywhere -> monopoly rents.
Labour and environmental standards: "race to bottom" — firms move to lowest-regulation countries.
Cultural homogenisation: US cultural exports (McDonald''s, Hollywood) displace local cultures.
Financial contagion: 2008 US housing crisis -> global financial crisis instantly.
Vulnerability: COVID-19 exposed fragility of just-in-time global supply chains.

BACKLASH:
Brexit: UK voted to leave EU (2016). Sovereignty and immigration concerns.
Trump tariffs: US-China trade war. Reshoring discourse.
Nearshoring: move supply chains closer to home (friend-shoring) for resilience.
De-globalisation: some data shows globalisation slowing since 2008.
But: trade as % of GDP still high. Global trade still growing in services/digital.
